comments.author: @jackmorganfiftyfive
comments.text: I am of the opinion that no one needed to be evacuated from St Kilda. Yes, it was covered in fog and unreachable for months, but the government wasted an important opportunity here. The island could have been an important forward naval base in the Atlantic, with its protected internal bay. The bay could have been deepened to allow warships and submarines to enter. That would have also given the local villagers an economy with produce and services. Now its only a forward listening post but it could have been so much more...

comments.text: An interesting aspect is the survival into the early 1700s of a mixed Druidic/Catholic faith, several altars to which they sacrificed sheep & a stone circle on the smaller island where the islands Druid lived. These things were recorded in books in the years before a protestant missionary arrived to reform it all. The stone circle was destroyed however many of the altars remain as do a number of shrines like the milking stone & holy wells. This is oldest Druidic survival in the UK.

comments.author: @brucewalker5890
comments.text: Sadly most of those evacuated died of diseases like measles. A bunch of St Kildans sailed to Australia circa 1860s. They settled in an area of Melbourne now the suburb named St Kilda after them. A documentary was made of the 1930 evacuation and may be available on U Tube. The big issue on the Island was the massive mortality rate of babies born. It was eventually attributed to birthing practices of islanders who unwittingly introduced tetanus to their babies. Very sad. I believe Thomas Cook took tourists to the Island from around 1820.

replies.author: @brucewalker5890
